<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader||SPHERICAL HARMONICS|657}}</noinclude>The function <math>\text{J}_m(\rho)</math> is called Bessel's function of order <math>m</math>, and <math>\text{J}_0(\rho)</math> simply Bessel's function; the series are convergent for all finite values of <math>\rho</math>.

The equation (29) is unaltered by changing <math>m</math> into <math>-m</math>, it follows that <math>\text{J}_{-m}(\rho)</math> is a second solution of (29), thus in general
{{block center|<math>u = \text{AJ}_m(\rho) + \text{BJ}_{-m}(\rho)</math>}}
is the complete primitive of (29). However, in the most important case, that in which <math>m</math> is an integer, the solutions <math>\text{J}_{-m}(\rho)</math>, <math>\text{J}_m(\rho)</math> are not distinct, for <math>\text{J}_{-m}(\rho)</math> may be written in the form
{{block center|<math>\left(\frac{\rho}{2}\right)^{-m} \sum_{n=0}^{m-1} \frac{(-1)^n}{\Pi(n-m)\Pi(n)} \left(\frac{\rho}{2}\right)^{2n}</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+(-1)^m \left(\frac{\rho}{2}\right)^m \sum_{p=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^p}{\Pi(m+p)\Pi(p)} \left(\frac{\rho}{2}\right)^{2p}</math>}}
now <math>\Pi(n-m)</math> is infinite when <math>m</math> is an integer, and <math>n < m</math>; thus the first part of the expression vanishes, and the second part is <math>(-1)^m\text{J}_m(\rho)</math>, hence when <math>m</math> is an integer <math>\text{J}_{-m}(\rho) = (-1)^m\text{J}_m(\rho)</math>, and the second solution remains to be found.

''Bessel's Functions of the Second Kind.''—When <math>m</math> is not a real integer, we have seen that any linear function of <math>\text{J}_m(\rho)</math>, <math>\text{J}_{-m}(\rho)</math> satisfies the equation of order <math>m</math>. The Bessel's function of the second kind of order <math>m</math> is defined as the particular linear function
{{block center|<math>\pi e^{m\pi\iota} \frac{\text{J}_{-m}(\rho) - \cos m\pi \,.\, \text{J}_m(\rho)}{\sin 2m\pi}</math>,}} and may be denoted by <math>\text{Y}_m(\rho)</math>. This definition has the advantage of giving a meaning to <math>\text{Y}_m(\rho)</math> in the case in which <math>m</math> is an integer, for it may be evaluated as a limiting form <math>0/0</math>, and the limit will satisfy the equation (29). The only failing case is when <math>m</math> is half an odd integer; in that case we take <math>\cos m\pi\,.\,\text{Y}_m(\rho)</math> as a second finite solution of the differential equation.

When <math>m</math> is an integer, we have

{{block center|<math>\text{Y}_m(\rho) = (-1)^m \frac{\pi}{2} \left\{ \frac{d\text{J}_{-m-\epsilon}}{d\epsilon} - (-1)^m \frac{d\text{J}_{m+\epsilon}}{d\epsilon} \right\} \epsilon = 0</math>}}

on carrying out the differentiations, and proceeding to the limit we find

{{block center|<math>\text{Y}_m(\rho) = \text{J}_m(\rho) \log \frac{2}{\rho} + \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{\rho}{2}\right)^m \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} [\dagger(n) + \dagger(m+n)] \frac{(-1)^n}{\Pi n(m+)\Pi(n)} \left(\frac{\rho}{2}\right)^{2n}</math>}}

{{block center|<math>+ \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{\rho}{2}\right)^{-m} \sum_{n=0}^{m-1} \frac{\Pi(m-n-1)}{\Pi(n)} \left(\frac{\rho}{2}\right)^{2n}</math>}}

where <math>\dagger(n)</math> denotes <math>\Pi'(n)/\Pi(n)</math>.

When <math>m = 0</math> we have the second solution of (30) given by

{{block center|<math>\text{Y}_0(\rho) = \text{J}_0(\rho) \log \frac{2}{\rho} + \sum_0^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n \dagger(n)}{\Pi(n)\Pi(n)} \left(\frac{\rho}{2}\right)^{2n}</math>.}}

21. ''Relations between Bessel's Functions of Different Orders.''—Since <math>e^z {}^{\cos}_{\sin} m\phi \cdot u_m(\rho)</math> satisfies Laplace's equation, it follows that <math>{}^{\cos}_{\sin} m\phi . u_m(\rho)</math> satisfies the differential equation {{block center|<math>\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} + u = 0.</math> (31)}}
The linear character of this equation shows that if <math>u</math> is any solution
{{block center|<math>f\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\right) u</math>}}
is also one, <math>f</math> denoting a rational integral function of the operators. Let <math>\xi</math>, <math>\eta</math> denote <math>x + \iota y</math>, <math>x - \iota y</math>, then since <math>\rho^{-m}\xi^m u_m(\sqrt{\xi\eta})</math> satisfies the differential equation, so also does
{{block center|<math>\xi^m \frac{\partial^p}{\partial\eta^p}\{\rho^{-m}u_m(\sqrt{\xi\eta})\},</math>}}
or
{{block center|<math>\xi^{m+p} \frac{d^p}{d(\rho^2)^p}\{\rho^{-m}u_m(\rho)\},</math>}}
thus we have
{{block center|<math>u_{m+p} = \text{C}\rho^{m+p} \frac{d^p}{d(\rho^2)^p} \left\{ \frac{u_m(\rho)}{\rho_m} \right\}</math>}}
where C is a constant. If <math>u_m(\rho) = \text{J}_m(\rho)</math>, we have <math>u_{m+p} = \text{J}_{m+p}(\rho)</math>, and by comparing the coefficients of <math>\rho^{m+p}</math>, we find <math>\text{C} = (-2)^p</math>, hence
{{block center|<math>\text{J}_{m+p}(\rho) = (-2)^p \rho^{m+p} \frac{d^p}{d(\rho^2)^p}\{\rho^{-m}\text{J}_m(\rho)\},</math>}}
and changing <math>m</math> into <math>-m</math>, we find
{{block center|<math>\text{J}_{p-m}(\rho) = (-2)^p \rho^{p-m} \frac{d^p}{d(\rho^2)^p}\{\rho^m \text{J}_{-m}(\rho)\}.</math>}} In a similar manner it can be proved that

{{block center|<math>\text{J}_{m\ p}(\rho) = 2^p\rho^{p-m}\frac{d^p}{d(\rho^2)^p}\{\rho^m\text{J}_m(\rho)\}.</math>}}

From the definition of <math>\text{Y}_m(\rho)</math>, and applying the above analysis, we prove that

{{block center|<math>\text{Y}_{m+p}(\rho) = (-2)^p\rho^{m+p}\frac{d^p}{d(\rho^2)^p}\{\rho^{-m}\text{Y}_m(\rho)\}</math>}}

and

{{block center|<math>\text{Y}_{m-p}(\rho) = 2^p\rho^{p-m}\frac{d^p}{d(\rho^2)^p}\{\rho^m\text{Y}_m(\rho)\}.</math>}}

As particular cases of the above formulae, we find

{{block center|<math>\text{J}_p(\rho) = (-2\rho)^p\frac{d^p}{d(\rho^2)^p}\text{J}_0(\rho),\ \text{Y}_p(\rho) = (-2\rho)^p\frac{d^p}{d(\rho^2)^p}\text{Y}_0(\rho)</math>}}

{{block center|<math>\text{J}_1(\rho) = -\frac{d\text{J}_0(\rho)}{d\rho},\ \text{Y}_1(\rho) = -\frac{d\text{Y}_0(\rho)}{d\rho}.</math>}}

22. ''Bessel's Functions as Coefficients in an Expansion.''—It is clear that <math>e^{\iota\rho\cos\phi} = e^{\iota x}</math> or <math>e^{\iota\rho\sin\phi} = e^{\iota y}</math> satisfy the differential equation (31), hence if these exponentials be expanded in series of cosines and sines of multiples of <math>\phi</math>, the coefficients must be Bessel's functions, which it is easy to see are of the first kind. To expand <math>e^{\iota\rho\sin\phi}</math>, put <math>e^{\iota\phi} = t</math>, we have then to expand <math>e^{\frac{1}{2}\rho(t-t^{-1})}</math> in powers of <math>t</math>. Multiplying together the two absolutely convergent series

{{block center|<math>e^{\frac{1}{2}\rho t} = \sum\frac{1}{m!}\left(\frac{\rho}{2}\right)^m t^m,\ e^{-\frac{1}{2}\rho t^{-1}} = \sum\frac{(-1)^m}{m!}\left(\frac{1}{2\rho}\right)\ t^m_m,</math>}} we obtain for the coefficient of <math>t^m</math> in the product
{{block center|<math>\frac{\rho^m}{2^m m!}\left\{1-\frac{\rho^2}{2.2m+2}+\frac{\rho^4}{2.4.2m+2.2m+4}-\dots\right\}</math> or <math>\text{J}_m(\rho)</math>,}}
hence
{{block center|<math>\left.\begin{array}{r}e^{\frac{1}{2}\rho(t-t^{-1})}=\text{J}_0(\rho)+t\text{J}_1(\rho)+\dots+t^m\text{J}_m(\rho)+\dots\\ -t^{-1}\text{J}_1(\rho)+\dots+(-1)^m t^{-m}\text{J}_m(\rho)\end{array}\right\}</math> (32)}}
{{block center|<math>=\sum_{-\infty}^{\infty}t^m\text{J}_m(\rho)</math>}}
the Bessel's functions were defined by Schlömilch as the coefficients of the powers of <math>t</math> in the expansion of <math>e^{\frac{1}{2}\rho(t-t^{-1})}</math>, and many of the properties of the functions can be deduced from this expansion. By differentiating both sides of (32) with respect to <math>t</math>, and equating the coefficients of <math>t^{m-1}</math> on both sides, we find the relation
{{block center|<math>\text{J}_{m-1}(\rho)+\text{J}_{m+1}(\rho)=\frac{2m}{\rho}\text{J}_m(\rho),</math>}}
which connects three consecutive functions. Again, by differentiating both sides of (32) with respect to <math>\rho</math>, and equating the coefficients of corresponding terms, we find
{{block center|<math>2\frac{d\text{J}_m(\rho)}{d\rho}=\text{J}_{m\ 1}(\rho)-\text{J}_{m+1}(\rho).</math>}}

In (32), let <math>t=e^{\iota\phi}</math>, and equate the real and imaginary parts, we have then
{{block center|<math>\cos(\rho\sin\phi)=\text{J}_0(\rho)+2\text{J}_2(\rho)\cos 2\phi+2\text{J}_3(\rho)\cos 3\phi+\dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\sin(\rho\sin\phi)=2\text{J}_1(\rho)\sin\phi+2\text{J}_3(\rho)\sin 3\phi+\dots</math>}}
we obtain expansions of <math>\cos(\rho\cos\phi)</math>, <math>\sin(\rho\cos\phi)</math>, by changing <math>\phi</math> into <math>\tfrac{1}{2}-\phi</math>. On comparing these expansions with Fourier's series, we find expressions for <math>\text{J}_m(\rho)</math> as definite integrals, thus {{block center|<math>\text{J}_0(\rho) = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^\pi \cos\,(\rho\sin\phi)d\phi,\ \text{J}_m(\rho) = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^\pi \cos\,(\rho\sin\phi)\cos m\phi d\phi\ (m\ \text{even})</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\text{J}_m(\rho) = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^\pi \sin\,(\rho\sin\phi)\sin m\phi d\phi\ (m\ \text{odd}).</math>}}
It can easily be deduced that when <math>m</math> is any positive integer
{{block center|<math>\text{J}_m(\rho) = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^\pi \cos\,(m\phi - \rho\sin\phi)d\phi.</math>}}

23. ''Bessel's Functions as Limits of Legendre's Functions.''—The system of orthogonal surfaces whose parameters are cylindrical co-ordinates may be obtained as a limiting case of those whose parameters are polar co-ordinates, when the centre of the spheres moves off to an indefinite distance from the portion of space which is contemplated. It would therefore be expected that the normal forms <math>e^{\pm\lambda z}\text{J}_m(\lambda\rho){}^{\cos}_{\sin}m\phi</math> would be derivable as limits of <math>{}^{r^n}_{r^{-n-1}}\text{P}^m_n(\cos\theta){}^{\cos}_{\sin}m\phi</math>, and we shall show that this is actually the case. If O be the centre of the spheres, take as new origin a point C on the axis of <math>z</math>, such that <math>\text{OC} = a</math>; let P be a point whose polar co-ordinates are <math>r</math>, <math>\theta</math>, <math>\phi</math> referred to O as origin, and cylindrical co-ordinates <math>\rho</math>, <math>z</math>, <math>\phi</math> referred to C as origin; we have
{{block center|<math>\rho = r\sin\theta,\ z = r\cos\theta - a,\ \text{hence}\ \left(\frac{r}{a}\right)^n\text{P}_n(\cos\theta) = \sec^n\theta\left(1 + \frac{z}{a}\right)^n\text{P}_n(\cos\theta).</math>}}
Now let O move off to an infinite distance from C, so that <math>a</math> becomes<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
